content: Liver spots, also referred to as age spots, sun spots, lentigos, or senile/solar lentigines, are pigmented blemishes that appear on the skin. They can vary in color, ranging from light brown to black, and are most commonly found on areas of the body that are frequently exposed to sunlight. These areas include the hands, face, shoulders, arms, and forehead. Despite their name, liver spots have no connection to the liver or its function. The term liver spots originates from the resemblance of their coloration to that of the liver. Starting around the age of 40, the skin's ability to repair itself from sun damage diminishes, making liver spots increasingly common in older individuals, particularly those who spend significant time outdoors. In some cases, emotional stress has been observed to contribute to the proliferation of these spots. For the vast majority of individuals, liver spots are harmless and do not require medical treatment. However, in rare instances, they may obscure the detection of skin cancers, which necessitates careful monitoring. Some individuals may find liver spots cosmetically undesirable and choose to have them removed. Removal options include cryotherapy, which involves freezing the spots, or laser treatment, which uses focused light to target the pigmentation. During a physical examination, liver spots are typically identified through visual inspection of the skin. Dermatologists may refer to resources such as dermatology atlases to confirm the diagnosis and differentiate liver spots from other skin conditions.
